entry: Genus of woody perennial flowering plants in the family [[Rosaceae]], or the [[Flower|flower]] it bears. There are over 300 species and tens of thousands of [[Cultivar|cultivars]]. Plants range from trailing and erect [[Shrub|shrubs]] to climbers up to 7 m (23 ft) tall, and many species bear sharp prickles on their stems, often called thorns. Flowers are usually large and showy, in colors from white through pink, red, orange and yellow, and most species have five petals. Most species are native to Asia, with fewer native to Europe, North America and Northwest Africa. Species [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridize]] readily, which has produced the wide range of garden roses. Insects pollinate roses, and the hips, or fruits, of some species, such as the dog rose, are very rich in [[Vitamin C]]. Birds such as [[Thrush (bird)|thrushes]] eat the hips and disperse the seeds, while [[Deer|deer]] frequently browse the plants.

American actress and activist. After a brief role in *Encino Man* (1992), McGowan won recognition for the dark comedy *The Doom Generation* (1995). She broke through in the [[Horror film|horror film]] *Scream* (1996) and played Paige Matthews on the television series *Charmed* (2001–2006). In 2017, [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named her one of the Silence Breakers, its Person of the Year, for speaking out about [[Sexual assault|sexual assault]] and harassment, including the cases involving [[Harvey Weinstein]] and the [[MeToo movement]]. Her 2018 memoir, *Brave*, followed.

American television [[Sitcom|sitcom]]. Created by Matt Williams, it aired on ABC from October 18, 1988, to May 20, 1997, and was briefly revived in 2018. [[Roseanne Barr]] starred as Roseanne Conner, a working-class mother in the fictional town of Lanford, [[Illinois]]. The series received generally positive reviews and reached No. 1 in the Nielsen ratings in 1989–1990. ABC canceled the revival on May 29, 2018, after Barr likened former Obama administration official Valerie Jarrett to *Planet of the Apes* on Twitter. The spin-off *The Conners* ran from October 2018 to 2025.

American actress, comedian, writer and producer. She began in [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up comedy]] and became widely known as the lead of the ABC sitcom *Roseanne* (1988–1997; 2018), for which she received an Emmy and a Golden Globe. Plans for further seasons of the 2018 revival were dropped after a tweet by Barr that many commentators condemned as racist; she later called it a "bad joke." Her comeback comedy special, *Cancel This!*, was released on Fox Nation in 2023.

Fragrant evergreen shrub in the [[Lamiaceae|mint family]], native to the Mediterranean region. Its needle-like leaves are commonly used as a flavoring, and the plant has numerous [[Cultivar|cultivars]]. Upright forms can reach 1.2–1.8 meters (4–6 ft) tall. Its flowers are purple, or sometimes white, pink or blue. Carl Linnaeus first described it in 1753 as *Rosmarinus officinalis*. In 2017, molecular phylogenetic evidence led to its reclassification into [[Salvia]] as *Salvia rosmarinus*.

1968 American supernatural [[Horror film|horror film]] by [[Roman Polanski]], adapted from Ira Levin's 1967 novel. [[Mia Farrow]] plays Rosemary, a newlywed in [[Manhattan]] who begins to suspect that her elderly neighbors are Satanists with sinister intentions toward her and her baby. Produced by William Castle, it was Polanski's first American production. It premiered on June 12, 1968, and grossed over $30 million. Ruth Gordon won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. In 2014 the film was selected for preservation in the [[Library of Congress]]'s National Film Registry.

Granodiorite stele inscribed with three versions of a decree issued in 196 BC during the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt, on behalf of King Ptolemy V Epiphanes. The top and middle texts are in [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptian]], using [[Egyptian hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic]] and Demotic scripts, and the bottom text is in [[Ancient Greek]]. The versions differ only slightly, which made the stone the key to deciphering the Egyptian scripts. French officer Pierre-François Bouchard found it in July 1799 near Rashid (Rosetta) in the [[Nile|Nile]] Delta during France's invasion of Egypt. Under the terms of the Capitulation of Alexandria, the British took it to London in 1801, and it has been displayed at the [[British Museum]] since 1802. Jean-François Champollion announced the transliteration of the Egyptian scripts in 1822. Though not unique, it was essential to the modern understanding of ancient Egyptian literature and civilization.

Spiritual and cultural movement influenced by [[Hermeticism]] and Esoteric Christianity that arose in early modern Europe. It began in the early 17th century after the publication of several anonymous texts announcing a new [[Secret society|secret society]]. The movement is symbolized by the Rose Cross or Rosy Cross. Two anonymous manifestos appeared between 1610 and 1615, and a third, the *Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz*, followed in 1616. Initially the Rosicrucians were not supposed to be real people, but the first real Rosicrucians appeared in the 18th century, probably in 1763. Later Rosicrucian-inspired organizations include the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (1887–1903).

American comedian and actress. She hosted the syndicated daytime [[Talk show|talk show]] *The Rosie O'Donnell Show* from 1996 to 2002, winning several Daytime Emmy Awards. During that period she gained the nickname "Queen of Nice" and a reputation for philanthropy. She came out as a [[Lesbian|lesbian]] in 2002 and became an advocate for lesbian rights and gay [[Adoption|adoption]]. In 2006 and 2007 she moderated *The View*, feuding publicly with Donald Trump. In early 2025 she moved to Ireland and applied for Irish citizenship through descent. In July 2025, Trump threatened to revoke her U.S. birthright citizenship.

Solid form of plant [[Resin|resin]] obtained from pine trees and other [[Conifer|conifers]], also called colophony. It consists mainly of resin acids, especially abietic acid, and ranges in color from yellow to black. Rubbed on bow hair, it increases friction for bowed string instruments. It has been used for centuries to caulk ships. Rosin is an ingredient in [[Ink|printing inks]], varnishes, [[Adhesive|adhesives]] and [[Soap|soap]], and it serves as a flux in [[Soldering|soldering]]. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approves it as a food additive.

American businessman and politician. He founded Electronic Data Systems in 1962, and [[General Motors]] bought a controlling interest in the company for $2.4 billion in 1984. He ran as an independent in the 1992 U.S. presidential election, winning over 19.7 million votes, or 18.9% of the popular vote, but no electoral votes. He ran again in 1996 as the nominee of the Reform Party and won 8.4% of the popular vote. Perot also campaigned on the [[Vietnam War|Vietnam War]] POW/MIA issue and opposed the [[Gulf War]] and the North American Free Trade Agreement. He died of [[Leukemia|leukemia]] in [[Dallas]].

Deep bay of the [[Southern Ocean]] in [[Antarctica]], between Victoria Land and Marie Byrd Land. It is the southernmost sea on Earth and covers 637,000 sq km (246,000 sq mi). The sea is named for British explorer James Clark Ross, who visited the area in 1841. Its southern part is covered by the Ross Ice Shelf, about 200 miles (320 km) from the [[South Pole]]. The sea is covered with ice for most of the year. Nutrient-rich water supports abundant [[Plankton|plankton]], and at least 10 mammal species, six bird species and 95 fish species live there. [[Roald Amundsen]] began his South Pole expedition in 1911 from the Bay of Whales. In 2016 an international agreement established the region as a marine park.

Port city on the [[Don (river)|Don River]] in southern Russia, the administrative center of Rostov Oblast. It lies 32 km (20 mi) from the [[Sea of Azov]] and has over one million residents. Established as a customs house in 1749 to control trade with Turkey, the settlement was renamed Rostov-on-Don in 1806. A railway to [[Kharkiv]] opened in 1870, and coal and iron ore supported heavy industry, while the harbor became a major hub for exporting [[Wheat|wheat]]. During [[World War I]], the [[German Empire]] briefly occupied the city in 1918. The [[Russian Civil War]] saw Whites and Reds contest the city, and Nazi German forces occupied it in 1941 during [[World War II]].

Movement of an object that leaves at least one point unchanged, also called rotational motion. In two dimensions, a plane figure rotates clockwise or counterclockwise around a center of rotation. In three dimensions, a solid rotates around an axis of rotation. A rotation about an internal axis through the body's center of mass is called a spin, and Earth's rotation defines the geographical poles. A rotation around an external axis is a [[Orbit|revolution]], such as [[Earth's orbit]] around the [[Sun]]. Mathematically, a rotation is a rigid body movement that, unlike a translation, keeps at least one point fixed. Rotations around a point or axis form a [[Group (mathematics)|group]], and any spatial rotation can be decomposed into rotations around the x, y and z axes.

Genus of double-stranded [[RNA]] viruses in the family Reoviridae, and the most common cause of [[Diarrhea|diarrheal]] disease among infants and young children. Nearly every child is infected at least once by age five, and immunity develops with each infection. The virus is transmitted by the fecal–oral route. It infects the cells lining the [[Small intestine|small intestine]], causing [[Gastroenteritis|gastroenteritis]]. Rotavirus was discovered in 1973 by Ruth Bishop and her colleagues, and it accounts for about one-third of hospitalizations for severe diarrhea in infants and children. Rotavirus caused an estimated 151,714 deaths from diarrhea among children under 5 worldwide in 2019. The genus includes 11 [[Species|species]], and RVA causes more than 90% of human infections. In countries that added rotavirus [[Vaccination|vaccine]] to routine childhood immunization, incidence and severity have declined significantly. Public health campaigns emphasize oral rehydration therapy.

Ashkenazi Jewish noble banking family originally from [[Frankfurt]], Germany. Mayer Amschel Rothschild, a court factor to the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel, established the family's banking business in the 1760s. He passed his wealth to five sons, who set up banks in Paris, Frankfurt, [[London]], [[Vienna]] and [[Naples]]. The family was elevated to noble rank in the [[Holy Roman Empire]] and the [[United Kingdom]]. In the 19th century it held the largest private fortune in the world, and it dominated European finance from the 1820s to the 1870s, when joint-stock banks broke its hegemony. Today its assets span financial services, real estate, mining, energy, agriculture and winemaking. The family has frequently been the subject of antisemitic conspiracy theories.

American review-aggregation website for film and television. It was launched in August 1998 by three students at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. The idea came from Senh Duong, a fan of [[Jackie Chan]] who had collected reviews of his films. Since 2016 it has belonged to the Fandango ticketing company. A 2018 survey found that almost a third of U.S. adult moviegoers had consulted the site before going to the cinema. It has been criticized for oversimplifying reviews into fresh or rotten ratings, and for allowing studios to manipulate results by limiting early screenings to favorable critics.

Port city (pop., 2022: 655,468) in South Holland, the [[Netherlands]]. It is the country's second-largest city by population and its largest by area, at 319.4 sq km. Rotterdam's history goes back to 1270, when a dam was built on the Rotte, and it received city rights in 1340. Its merchants were involved in the [[Atlantic slave trade]] from the 1600s until 1814. The city is Europe's largest [[Port|seaport]] and has earned the nicknames "Gateway to Europe" and "Gateway to the World." Its city center was nearly destroyed by German bombing in [[World War II]], and its postwar architecture includes skyscrapers by Rem Koolhaas, Piet Blom and Ben van Berkel.

[[Casino|Casino]] game of chance, named after the French word for "little wheel." A player may bet on a single number, groups of numbers, red or black, odd or even, or high or low. The croupier spins the wheel one way and a ball the other way around a track, and the ball falls into a numbered and colored pocket. Winning bets are then paid. The game was likely developed from the Italian game Biribi. Some accounts credit [[Blaise Pascal]] with a primitive form in the 17th century, but his role is disputed. The game has been played in its present form as early as 1796 in Paris. In 1843, François and Louis Blanc introduced the single-zero wheel at Bad Homburg, and it became the premier game at [[Monte Carlo]]. In the United States, the double-zero wheel remained dominant. House edges are about 2.70% for European roulette and 5.26% for American roulette.

Computer networking device that forwards data packets between [[Computer network|computer networks]], including the global [[Internet]]. A router reads the network address in each packet header and uses its routing table or policy to send the packet toward its destination. Home and small-office routers forward IP packets between home computers and the Internet, while enterprise routers connect large networks to core routers on the [[Optical fiber|optical fiber]] backbone. Routers are mostly purpose-built embedded systems, though early models ran software on a general-purpose CPU. Advanced models use application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) to improve performance and add filtering and firewall functions. The first true IP router was developed by Ginny Travers at BBN from 1975 to 1976 as part of a DARPA-initiated effort that created the TCP/IP architecture.

English actor, comedian and writer. He first gained success on the sketch comedy show *Not the Nine O'Clock News* (1979–1982), then starred in the sitcoms *Blackadder* and *Mr. Bean* (1990–1995), the latter bringing him international fame. He appeared in the [[James Bond]] film *Never Say Never Again* (1983) and played the title role in the *Johnny English* spy spoof films. Atkinson won British Academy Television Awards in 1981 and 1990, and he was appointed CBE in 2013 for services to drama and charity.

[[Sport|Sport]] of racing boats using oars, called crew in the [[United States]]. In sculling, each rower holds two oars, while in sweeping each rower holds one oar with both hands. Boat classes range from single sculls to eights, which carry eight rowers and a coxswain. Most elite racing takes place on calm-water courses 2 km (1.2 mi) long with buoyed lanes. Modern competitive rowing can be traced to the early 17th century, when professional watermen held races on the [[River Thames]] in London, often with prizes from the London guilds. The oldest surviving race, Doggett's Coat and Badge, was first contested in 1715 and is still held annually from [[London Bridge]] to Chelsea. Men have rowed at the Olympics since 1900 and women since 1976.

Irish football pundit and former player. He captained Manchester United from 1997 to 2005, helping the club win seven [[Premier League|Premier League]] titles, four FA Cups and the [[UEFA Champions League]]. For the Republic of Ireland, he was sent home from the [[FIFA World Cup]] in 2002 after a dispute with manager Mick McCarthy. He later managed Sunderland, which won promotion to the Premier League under him, and Ipswich Town. He has since worked as a television analyst and was inducted into the Premier League Hall of Fame in 2021.

American singer, songwriter and guitarist, known for his powerful voice and dark, emotional ballads. Born in [[Texas]], he was signed by Sam Phillips of Sun Records in 1956 after being urged by [[Johnny Cash]]. His greatest success came with Monument Records, and from 1960 to 1966, 22 of his singles reached the Billboard top 40, including "Only the Lonely" (1960) and "Oh, Pretty Woman" (1964). After a late-1980s resurgence, he co-founded the Traveling Wilburys with [[George Harrison]], [[Bob Dylan]], [[Tom Petty]] and Jeff Lynne in 1988. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1987.

Protected [[National park|national park]] in [[New South Wales]], [[Australia]], about 29 km (18 mi) south of central [[Sydney]]. Covering 151 sq km (58 sq mi), it was founded by Sir John Robertson, acting premier of New South Wales, and proclaimed on April 26, 1879, the first national park in Australia. It was proclaimed seven years after [[Yellowstone National Park]] and 11 years before [[Yosemite National Park]]. It was renamed in 1955 after [[Elizabeth II]] passed through by train during her 1954 tour. The park lies on traditional lands of the Dharawal people and has over 100 km (62 mi) of walking tracks.
